title: Victorian water tables fell about 1 m after 1997 and stayed low at equal rain; larger falls went with larger runoff losses, but the pre-1997 water-table relation predicts none of the loss (36 basins)
abstract: Question: after 1997, south-east Australian runoff fell below each catchment's 1951-1996 rainfall-runoff relation and stayed low. Earlier work found a baseflow fingerprint and faster recession, but no study used groundwater levels. Did the shallow water table fall where runoff fell, and does the water-table level control rain-adjusted runoff? Approach: we used 3,992 Victorian WMIS bore records (782 shallow bores after quality control) and 36 CAMELS-AUS v2.03 catchments with 2 or more bores within 5 km. We compared a catchment water-table index with the annual runoff residual from a 1951-1996 rain and temperature fit. The plan was written before groundwater results; lag, rain-memory, control and recovery tests are post hoc. Results: water tables fell from 1997, were a median 1.13 m below the 1985-1996 level in 2010-2021, and in 91% of 181 bores stayed below their own pre-1997 rain response. Catchments with larger falls had larger runoff deficits (Spearman rho +0.61, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.77; +0.62 with rain-change control). This link weakened to +0.31 (-0.05 to 0.71) with aridity and runoff-ratio controls. Inside catchments, the 1985-1996 water table did not predict rain-adjusted runoff (previous-year slope -0.21 SD/m, -0.58 to +0.15; a slope of about +1.0 is necessary). Thus the pre-1997 relation predicts none of the 2010-end deficit (-21%, -61 to +15%), and the water table absorbs only 9-14% of the post-1997 step. A weak positive groundwater slope and a strong multi-year rain memory appeared only after 1997. Runoff and water table recovered by similar fractions in 2011-2013 (40% and 47%). Conclusion: the water-table fall shares the start, persistence and spatial pattern of the runoff loss but is not a fixed control on it; a common driver or a threshold change such as stream-aquifer disconnection fits better. Limitations: few catchments, spatial confounding with aridity, bores away from streams, no pumping or land-use separation, annual scale only.
